headline: Oregon City Council certifies data center cap for November ballot — Vantage site purchase agreement expires end of September, six weeks before vote
paragraphs: Residents of Oregon, Ohio — a city of approximately 20,000 in eastern Lucas County — are collecting voter signatures for a proposed city charter amendment that would limit data center capacity within Oregon's city limits to 25 megawatts. The group Protect Oregon, Ohio has until August 5, 2026 to deliver approximately 1,700 valid signatures to the Lucas County Board of Elections to qualify the amendment for the November 3 ballot. If enough signatures are verified and voters approve the measure, it would restrict the scale of future data center development and steer projects toward brownfield and industrial sites rather than farmland — without banning data centers outright. Petition organizer James Davis has said the effort aims to prevent large-scale data center development from displacing residential and agricultural areas of the community.

City officials in Oregon confirmed Vantage Data Centers as the prospective developer for the project that triggered the petition drive, with a proposed site near Wynn and Corduroy Roads in Oregon. Vantage Data Centers, backed by Silver Lake Partners, is one of the largest hyperscale data center developers in North America — the proposed campus calls for three buildings at a scale approaching $2 billion in investment, with 20 to 30 permanent employees and the potential for multiple end users per building. Separately, a statewide constitutional amendment to ban data centers over 25MW failed to gather sufficient signatures by its July 1 deadline — Conserve Ohio (formerly Ohio Residents for Responsible Development) collected approximately 70,000 of the required 413,488 signatures statewide, with Lucas County leading all Ohio counties at 6,482; the statewide effort continues on a 2027 track.

Two significant developments followed in the week before the August 5 petition deadline. Oregon City Council narrowly rejected an emergency ordinance that would have extended key contingencies tied to pipeline access, emissions approvals, and electrical infrastructure for the Vantage project. Three council members supported the extension; Beth Ackerman and Paul Gibbs voted against; Dennis Walendzak abstained; Dave Andrus was absent. WTOL reported the vote 'puts data center project in doubt.' Developer Will Turner of Capacity LLC — whose site purchase agreement runs through end of September 2026 — told council the project needs more time to complete FirstEnergy permitting, noting the project is running approximately six months behind schedule. Oregon Mayor Steven Salander issued a formal proclamation on July 13 stating Oregon will follow its own Master Plan, which designates land east of Wynn Road and north of Corduroy Road for residential use only — a direct conflict with the proposed data center footprint. On July 29, petition organizer James Davis confirmed signature collection was still in progress, with plans to gather signatures at a Navarre Avenue flea market on August 2.

The Blade published 'Oregon voters could decide data center size limits' on August 7, 2026 — the day after the August 5 petition deadline. The headline confirms that the Protect Oregon, Ohio petition drive submitted signatures to the Lucas County Board of Elections, with the charter amendment now moving to an LCBOE verification process to confirm whether approximately 1,700 valid signatures meet the qualifying threshold for the November 3 ballot. If verified, Oregon voters will be the first in Lucas County to decide on a cap on data center capacity — a 25MW limit that would restrict but not prohibit data center development within the city. The Vantage Data Centers project (three buildings near Wynn and Corduroy Roads, approaching $2 billion in scale) remains constrained by the council's earlier rejection of the timeline extension; developer Will Turner's site purchase agreement runs through end of September 2026. LCBOE signature verification and any subsequent legal challenges are the next milestones.

The Blade published 'Oregon amendment advances as organizers plan more data center ballot measures' on August 13, 2026 — a material development extending the story's significance beyond Oregon city limits. The headline confirms the petition has cleared initial procedural hurdles and is advancing toward LCBOE signature verification for the November 3 ballot. More consequentially, the reporting indicates Protect Oregon Ohio organizers are now planning to pursue data center ballot measures in additional jurisdictions beyond Oregon, signaling that the charter amendment model could spread to other communities across Lucas County and northwest Ohio facing large-scale data center proposals. No LCBOE formal signature verification result has been publicly announced as of August 16; the Vantage Data Centers site purchase agreement remains active through end of September 2026.

The Lucas County Board of Elections completed its signature verification review and confirmed that the Protect Oregon Ohio petition contains a sufficient number of valid signatures to advance the 25MW data center cap charter amendment to the ballot, as reported by The Press (presspublications.com). The United Neighbors of Oregon group submitted approximately 2,100 signatures, surpassing the 1,700-signature threshold. Under Ohio constitutional provisions governing municipal charter amendments, the Oregon city council now has a 60- to 120-day window to certify the measure for placement on the November 3 ballot, with 60 days equating to approximately September 4. Oregon voters will now be positioned to be the first in Lucas County — and among the first in Ohio — to directly vote on a cap limiting data center capacity within a municipality. The Vantage Data Centers site purchase agreement (three-building campus near Wynn and Corduroy Roads, approaching $2 billion in investment) remains active through end of September 2026; the measure's trajectory toward the November ballot introduces ballot risk into the project timeline.

Oregon City Council voted unanimously on August 19, 2026 to certify the Protect Oregon Ohio charter amendment for placement on the November 3 ballot — a formal resolution satisfying Ohio's constitutional requirement for municipal charter amendments and completing the procedural path to a public vote. The unanimous vote represents a notable shift from the council's earlier divided posture on data center policy; no member sought to delay or block certification. With certification now complete, the Vantage Data Centers project faces two concurrent legal clocks: the site purchase agreement held by developer Will Turner's Capacity LLC expires end of September 2026, approximately six weeks from now, while the ballot measure does not reach voters until November 3 — a gap of nearly five weeks between the expiration of the purchase agreement and the public vote. A 'yes' vote on November 3 would enact the 25MW cap; Vantage's proposed three-building campus would require substantially more capacity than the cap permits.
why_it_matters: The Oregon charter amendment effort is the first concrete local-government-level pushback against data center development in Lucas County, arriving precisely as the Regional Growth Partnership, JobsOhio, and the Toledo CIC are actively marketing the region's data center readiness to hyperscale investors. If the petition qualifies and voters approve it in November, Oregon would be the first municipality in northwest Ohio to cap data center capacity — a signal that community resistance to large-scale energy-intensive development is a variable in Toledo-area site selection. The timing compounds the broader statewide data center investment thesis: JobsOhio's AI-Ready Ohio initiative and the Gordie Howe Bridge freight corridor are both active in the same market window where local opposition is crystallizing. The August 5 signature deadline and the November 3 ballot — which already carries TPS, public safety, library, and Imagination Station levies — make this a watch-list item for the remainder of the summer.
